title: Migrants
last: PEACEMAKERS TREAT NO ONE AS AN ENEMY.

lines: A FAMILY LEAVES IN THE NIGHT.
cards: A family leaves home by night. The father has been warned in a dream that a ruler wants to kill their child. They don't wait for morning.

They take the baby and his mother and head for another country, Egypt, where they'll live as foreigners until it's safe to come back. That's Matthew's Gospel, and in Catholic art it's called the Flight into Egypt.
For a time, the Holy Family were people on the move. Pope Francis has pointed to that family when speaking about migrants and refugees, and he boiled the Church's response down to four verbs.

teach.b: First, welcome. The door has to open before anything else can happen. Francis talks about safe and legal ways in, so that people aren't pushed into the hands of smugglers.
Behind it is Jesus's own line in the Douay-Rheims, from the judgment scene in Matthew: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Second, protect.
Once someone has arrived, they're often at the mercy of others: employers who don't pay, landlords who exploit, people who take their papers.
Protecting means defending their rights and safety, especially for children.
Third, promote. Not just keeping people alive, but helping them flourish: work, language, school, the chance to use their gifts. A doctor driving a taxi for years is a loss for everyone.
Fourth, integrate. Not swallowing people up so they forget where they came from, and not leaving them on a separate island.
Francis describes a two-way process, where newcomers and the community that receives them both change and both are enriched. Now the balance, because the Catholic tradition holds two things together.

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: The Catechism says that more prosperous nations are obliged, as far as they are able, to welcome the foreigner in search of security and a livelihood.

It also says that political authorities may set legal conditions on immigration for the common good, and that immigrants are obliged to respect the laws and heritage of the country that receives them.
Catholics argue, sometimes sharply, about where that balance falls. But the four verbs sit underneath the argument: whatever the policy, the person in front of you is a person.

how: Catholic parishes and charities welcome and accompany migrants and refugees through legal aid, language classes, housing help and resettlement work, and the Church keeps a yearly World Day of Migrants and Refugees.

o: visitors on a short trip to another country
people who move to live in another country
people who move often from house to house

p: the door opens: safe ways in
both sides change and are enriched

s: in Matthew, the Holy Family flees to Egypt
warned in a dream, Joseph takes the child and his mother by night.
the Catechism says nations may set no conditions on immigration
it says authorities may set legal conditions for the common good, and prosperous nations must welcome as far as they are able.
for Francis, integrate means newcomers should forget where they came from
he describes a two-way process where both sides are enriched.

games.q: a refugee family has just moved in down the street. they're safe now. according to Francis's four verbs, is the work done?
o: no: there's still protect, promote and integrate.
it's the government's job, not a neighbor's.
games.why: welcome is only the first verb. Francis adds protect, promote and integrate: rights, room to flourish, and a two-way belonging.

practice: Think of the people around you who came from somewhere else, a coworker, a classmate's parent, the person who cuts your hair, a family at church, and pick one: which of the four verbs could you offer them?
If no one comes to mind, think of a local group that serves migrants, and what it might need. If you pray, pray for families on the move; if you don't, simply hold that one person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Migrants. People on the move, like the Holy Family in Egypt, and the four verbs Francis gave for meeting them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: four verbs. Welcome, protect, promote and integrate, whatever the policy. Rest well.
